chunks: Abu Ali ibn Rashid said to me: I said to him, 'You ordered me to fulfill your affair and take your right, so I informed your mawali (clients/followers) of that.' Some of them said to me, 'And what is his right?' So I did not know what to answer him. He said, 'Khums is obligatory upon them.' I said, 'In what?' He said, 'In their goods and their estates.' He said, 'And the merchant [is subject to it] and the artisan with his hand.' He said, 'That is when it is possible for them after their expenses.'

He said: Ibrahim ibn Muhammad al-Hamdani wrote to him, 'Ali read to me the letter of your father regarding what he made obligatory upon the owners of estates: that he made obligatory upon them half of the sixth (one-twelfth) after the expenses, and that upon one whose estate does not cover its own expenses, there is no half of the sixth, nor anything else.' So there was a difference of opinion among us regarding that, and they said: 'Khums is obligatory upon the estates after the expenses, which are the expenses of the estate and its tax, not the expenses of the man and his family.' So he wrote and Ali ibn Mahziyar read it: 'Upon him is Khums after his expenses and the expenses of his family, and after the tax of the ruler.'
ai.seo_question: What are the conditions and deductions for Khums on agricultural land and trade goods in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* highlights the jurisprudential debate (*ikhtilaf*) among Shia scholars regarding the deduction of personal and familial expenses (*ma'unah*) before calculating Khums on agricultural yields and trade profits. While some limited deductions to estate costs, the prevailing view affirmed that Khums is due after deducting both the owner's livelihood needs and the sovereign's tax (*kharaj*), reflecting the practical application of the 'fifth' on surplus wealth.
